To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Rab3 is a Ca2+-sensitive protein that regulates short-term plasticity at the cholinergic synapse of the buccala ganglion of Aplysis californica.
the Rab proteins are involved in short-term plasticity, and that this involvement is Ca2+-dependent.
the Rab3 proteins are GTPases that are involved in the control of neurotransmitter release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the Ca2+-dependent regulatory action of the small monomeric G-protein, Rab3, on neuroexocytic processes.
the molecular mechanisms of short-term plastic phenomena.
the role of Rab3 in short-term plasticity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Rab3 proteins may act as Ca2+-sensitive switches for the control of neurotransmitter release.
Rab3 proteins are not Ca2+-dependent, but Ca2+ is required to modulate the action of Rab3.
Rab3 is involved in the regulation and control of neurotransmission and that the Rab3 effectors, such as Rabphilin and rim, may be involved in this process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Rab3 is a negative regulator of neurotransmitter release, but this action is reduced during transient increases in intratermical Ca2+ concentration, thus allowing short-term plasticity.
Rab3 acts late, at the level of the exocytosis machinery, and that its activity is regulated by the Ca2+ concentration, which in turn is determined by the number of action potentials.
Rab3 is involved in the regulation not only of the release machinery but also of the intraterminal calcium concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GTP-bound Rab proteins can be regulated by Ca2+ in a manner that is consistent with a role in short-term plasticity.
the Rab3 proteins are Ca(2+)-dependent modulators of neuroexocytotic processes.
the GTP-bound form of Rab3 can be regulated by Ca2+ in a way that is relevant for synaptic transmission.
